questions.prompt: On a cold night, idli batter hasn’t fermented by morning. What is the most likely reason?
options: The microbes were too cold to work quickly
The batter had too much air
questions.explain: Many cooks put the batter in a warm spot, such as an oven with the light on.

questions.prompt: Why is boiled milk cooled to lukewarm before adding the curd starter?
options: Hot milk would kill the Lactobacillus bacteria

questions.prompt: In the kitchen, is each microbe activity something we WANT or something to PREVENT?
questions.explain: We control conditions to help friends and stop foes.

questions.prompt: Explain why the same warm kitchen that is great for fermenting batter is bad for storing cooked leftovers.
questions.modelAnswer: Warmth speeds up all microbes. In batter, we want the useful fermenting microbes to grow quickly. In cooked leftovers, warmth lets harmful bacteria multiply rapidly (doubling every 20–30 minutes), which can cause food poisoning. So leftovers should be cooled and refrigerated to slow bacterial growth, and reheated thoroughly before eating.

questions.prompt: Which is the safest way to keep leftover sambar overnight?
options: Leave it covered on the stove
Cool it quickly, refrigerate, and boil it again before serving
Leave it on the counter uncovered
Add extra salt and leave it out
questions.explain: Cooling slows microbes; boiling kills most before eating.

questions.prompt: Idli batter filled 1.2 L of a container at night and 2.1 L by morning. By what percentage did it rise?
Which microbes are at work in idli batter fermentation? Choose all that apply.
questions.explain: Lactic acid bacteria give sourness; yeasts help make gas.
